Australian Journal of Earth Sciences (2002) 49, 375–405
INTRODUCTION
This is the first of a number of detailed palaeomagnetic
studies on Carboniferous – Early Permian successions of
the Tamworth Belt in the southern New England Orogen,
covering the Rocky Creek, Werrie, Rouchel and Gresford
Blocks (Figure 1). The main objectives are to: (i) test on 
oroclinal bending of the Tamworth Belt; (ii) define a 
Late Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path for the New
England Orogen; (iii) compare this pole path with cratonic
Australian pole paths; and (iv) contribute to definition of
a representative pole path for Australia and (eastern)
Gondwanaland.
An extensive set of palaeomagnetic data for the Late
Palaeozoic of Australia has been accumulated over the 
past four decades and is now available through the global
palaeomagnetic database (McElhinny & Lock 1996), with
additional preliminary results in list form (Klootwijk
1996a). However ,there is still no consensus on the shape 
of Australia’s Late Palaeozoic pole path. Definition has 
suffered among others from general absence of a middle
Carboniferous stratigraphic record in cratonic sedi-
mentary basins and in the Tasmanides, from severe Early
Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Rocky 
Creek Block, northern Tamworth Belt, and the 
New England pole path*
C. T. KLOOTWIJK†
Australian Geodynamics Cooperative Research Centre, Geoscience Australia, GPO Box 378, 
Canberra, ACT 2601, Australia.
Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric results are presented for a Carboniferous
(Visean to Westphalian) succession of felsic, mainly ignimbritic, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks from
the Rocky Creek Block of the northern Tamworth Belt, southern New England Orogen. Detailed 
thermal demagnetisation of 734 samples from 64 sites show three groups of magnetic components
with low (<300°C), intermediate (300–600°C) and high (500–680°C) unblocking temperature ranges.
Well-defined primary magnetisations have been determined for 28 sites with evidence of four 
overprint phases. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent 
viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman
Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest
Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. Rock 
magnetic tests establish that the primary magnetisation carriers in the volcanic rocks are mainly 
magnetite (predominantly single domain, or pseudo-single domain, and little or no multidomain) and
hematite. Optimal magnetic cleaning is achieved at high to very high temperatures, with subtle,
but systematic, directional and statistical differences between primary components derived from
the mainly hematite fraction and pseudo-components derived from the mainly magnetite fraction.
The 28 primary magnetisation results are presented as six mean-site results, summarised below and
representing 25 sites, and three single-site results. Fold tests could be applied to five mean-site results.
These are all positive, but one of these results may represent a secondary magnetisation. The 
primary magnetisation results define a Visean to Westphalian pole path. This long pole path indi-
cates extensive latitudinal and rotational movement for the Rocky Creek Block, and potentially 
for the New England Orogen, as follows: (i) Yuendoo Rhyolite Member (Caroda Formation, Visean)
pole 235.8°E, 27.7°S, ED
95 = 9.0°, n = 3; (ii) Peri Rhyolite Member/Boomi Rhyolite Member (Clifden
Formation, Namurian, 318.0 ± 3.4 Ma) pole 177.4°E, 63.4°S, ED 95 = 5.2°, n = 3; (iii) tuffaceous beds above
Boomi Rhyolite Member (Clifden Formation?, Namurian) pole 162.2°E, 59.1°S, ED 95 = 10.2°, n = 3; [(iv)
upper Clifden Formation/lower Rocky Creek Conglomerate (Namurian/Westphalian) pole 95.3°E,
49.6°S, ED
95 = 8.1°, n = 3 (possible overprint)]; (v) Rocky Creek Conglomerate (Westphalian) pole
136.5°E, 57.6°S, ED 95 = 5.3°, n = 5; (vi) Lark Hill Formation (Westphalian) pole 127.0°E, 50.4°S, ED 95 = 4.8°,
n =8 .
KEY WORDS: Carboniferous, New England Orogen, palaeomagnetism, pole path, Rocky Creek Block,
Tamworth Belt.

### page_2
and middle Carboniferous overprinting related to the
Kanimblan and Alice Springs Orogenies, and from latest
Carboniferous – Early Permian overprinting probably
related to formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney
Basin system.
The Carboniferous – Early Permian succession of the
Tamworth Belt has several features favourable to defining
Australia’s Late Palaeozoic pole path, with others adding
complexity . The frequent presence of felsic volcanic rocks,
predominantly ignimbrites, favours determination of
primary magnetisations and SHRIMP U–Pb zircon ages.
Complexities such as, time of accretion, displacement with
respect to the Australian craton associated with formation
of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system and rota-
tional deformation associated with the Texas – Coffs
Harbour and Manning Oroclines need resolving before
Tamworth Belt palaeomagnetic data can be applied to
define the Australian pole path.
GEOLOGY
New England Orogen: overview
The New England Orogen is the easternmost, youngest
accreted segment of the Tasman Orogenic System or
Tasmanides, and forms an elongate belt stretching for more
than 2000 km from Townsville to Newcastle with a width of
up to 500 km. It is traditionally divided into a northern 
and southern part separated by the Mesozoic Surat and
Clarence–Moreton Basins: i.e. the northern New England
Orogen or Yarrol Orogen and the southern New England
Orogen or New England Orogen proper . The southern New
England Orogen is characterised by oroclines (Harrington
& Korsch 1985a): the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines 
in the north and the Manning Orocline in the south 
(Figure 1b). An oroclinal origin for the latter has been 
questioned (Lennox et al. 1997). The time of their formation
is also under dispute, but an Early Permian origin is most
likely (Harrington & Korsch 1985a; Korsch & Harrington
1987). The Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system is gen-
erally interpreted as a foreland basin to the New England
Orogen. The Tamworth Belt succession overthrusted the
Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system westward during
the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen
Orogeny (Harrington & Korsch 1985a, b; Harrington 1989;
Veevers et al. 1994a; Roberts & Geeve 1999), probably related
to accretion of the Gympie Terrane, the easternmost part
of the New England Orogen (Harrington & Korsch 1985a;
Harrington 1989).
The stratigraphy of the New England Orogen has been
traced back to the Early Cambrian, although preservation
of its early stratigraphic record is limited. The strati-
graphic succession is largely made up of Middle and Upper
Palaeozoic marine sediments with widespread magmatic
activity characterised by Carboniferous felsic volcanics 
and Permo-Triassic granites and felsic volcanics. Various
tectonostratigraphic subdivisions of the New England
Orogen have been proposed (Leitch 1974; Korsch 1977;
Roberts & Engel 1980; Cawood & Leitch 1985). The gross,
fourfold, subdivisions by Coney et al. (1990) and Scheibner
and Basden (1998) and the more detailed subdivision by
Aitchison and Flood (1995) are followed here (Figure 2). The
New England Orogen, or superterrane, can be divided from
west to east into the Proserpine (Connors–Auburn) mag-
matic belt, the Yarrol–Tamworth Terrane(s), the Wandilla–
Gwydir Terrane (Wandilla Tablelands Terrane: Scheibner
& Basden 1998), and the Nambucca and Gympie Terranes.
Palaeogeographically , and from west to east, these tectono-
stratigraphic terranes have been identified as a magmatic

arc (Connors–Auburn), a volcanic arc–forearc (Yarrol–

(Gympie).
Tamworth Belt: Upper Palaeozoic succession
The Tamworth Belt (Korsch 1977), the southern part of
the Yarrol–Tamworth Terrane, is characterised by two 
arc-related successions with distinct tectonostratigraphic
development. The older (Silurian?)–Devonian intra-oceanic
arc, the Gamilaroi Terrane (Flood & Aitchison 1992;
Aitchison & Flood 1995 figure 1), may already have been

### page_4
accreted to the cratonic Lachlan Orogen by the Late
Devonian (Famennian) and most probably by the middle
Carboniferous (Powell et al. 1990). The younger succession
is mainly made up of Upper Devonian to Carboniferous 
volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks with shelf-like character-
istics, deepening toward the east. The western continental-
arc source, the hypothetical Baldwin Arc (Veevers et al.
1982; McPhie 1987; Coney et al. 1990; Scheibner & Basden
1998; Roberts & Geeve 1999; Opdyke et al. 2000), evolved from
andesitic during the Devonian, into dacitic and then rhyo-
litic compositions during the Carboniferous. The location
of the arc has not been established in outcrop. It may have
been westward overthrust by the Tamworth Belt succession
during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–
Bowen Orogeny , or may have been displaced by dextral
strike-slip in the latest Carboniferous – Early Permian
(Harrington & Korsch 1985a; Harrington 1989; Korsch et al.
1997; Klootwijk et al. in press a).
The younger forearc basin succession starts with upper-
most Devonian deep-marine sediments, overlain by a Lower
Carboniferous shelfal succession with volcanic inter-
calations in its upper part. The upper Visean – lower
Namurian is characterised by a disconformity spanning a
hiatus of variable, up to 20 million years, duration along 
the belt (Opdyke et al. 2000). From middle to late Visean
onward the succession contains frequent felsic volcanic
(e.g. ignimbrites, ash-fall tuffs, lavas) and volcaniclastic
rocks (e.g. volcanogenically derived sandstones to mud-
stones). Local biostratigraphic control on the Carbon-
iferous succession is limited and globally correlatable
faunal control is sparse or unavailable. The widely occur-
ring felsic volcanics are prospective for SHRIMP U–Pb 
zircon studies and have been extensively dated (Claoué-
Long et al. 1995; Opdyke et al. 2000; Roberts et al. 1995a,
1995b). Compartmentalisation of this younger succession
has been recognised (Roberts & Engel 1987; Roberts et al.
1991). Roberts and Geeve (1999) identified seven blocks,
separated by fault zones/lineaments. From northwest to
southeast these are: the Rocky Creek, Werrie, Rouchel,
Gresford, Myall, southern Hastings, and northern Hastings
Blocks (Figure 1b). Stratigraphic development varies con-
siderably between the blocks and is detailed here for the
Rocky Creek Block.
Rocky Creek Block
The Carboniferous succession of the Rocky Creek Block 
is made up of a lower and an upper part separated by a 
late Visean to early Namurian hiatus of approximately 
10 million years duration according to SHRIMP U–Pb 
zircon data (Opdyke et al. 2000). The lower succession is
made up of Tournaisian marine shelf sediments, overlain
by Visean volcanogenically derived fluvial sediments with
intercalated tuffs and lavas. The upper succession is made
up of continental glaciogenic, volcaniclastic and fluvial
successions of Namurian and Westphalian to Stephanian
age (Opdyke et al. 2000).
378 C. T. Klootwijk

and intrusives are shown, but pre-Caroda and post-Lark Hill 
formations have been omitted for simplicity .

### page_5
The Carboniferous succession is exposed in three west-
vergent thrust sheets, identified here after Opdyke et al.
(2000), and from west to east, as the Darthula, Kathrose 
and Rocky Creek Thrust Sheets (Figure 3). The thrust
sheets were transported westward (Glen et al. 1993; Korsch
et al. 1997) during the Middle Triassic main phase of the
Hunter–Bowen Orogeny over distances up to 75–85 km
(Woodward 1995). Shortening estimates vary from at least
10 km (Wartenberg et al. 1999) to more than 30 km (Wang 
& Roberts 1999). Consequently , there is considerable 
stratigraphic variation between the volcano-sedimentary
successions of the three thrust sheets, complicating litho-
stratigraphic correlations. Recent detailed lithostrati-
graphic and magnetostratigraphic studies have led to a
revised correlation scheme (Opdyke et al. 2000) that is 
followed here, albeit with one proposed refinement. The
easternmost thrust sheet has the best exposure and the
most extensive outcrop throughout the Rocky Creek
Syncline (Figure 4). Its stratigraphy is described here for
reference purposes. The Rocky Creek Syncline is separated
by the Kathrose Fault from a narrow thrust slice of the
Kathrose Thrust Sheet to the west, which itself is separated
by the Trevallyn Fault from the westward adjacent, more
widely outcropping, Darthula Thrust Sheet (Figure 4).
The lower succession of the Rocky Creek Syncline is
made up of the Lower Carboniferous Luton, Namoi and
Caroda Formations. The Luton and Namoi Formations 
are of Tournaisian age in the west, but in the east the
Namoi Formation continues through to the middle Visean,
representing a local equivalent of the Caroda Formation.
Volcanic rocks first appear in the Caroda Formation, with
marine faunal evidence for a middle Visean age (Jenkins
et al. 1993; Roberts et al. 1993). The Caroda Formation is the
oldest formation sampled (Figure 5). It is characterised in
the northern Rocky Creek Block (Yeates 1970; Johnson 1971;
Stroud 1990a, b) by two dacitic to rhyodacitic tuffs, the
Yuendoo Rhyolite (Opdyke et al. 2000) and the West Lynne
Rhyodacite (Figure 6). The latter is affected by the erosional
disconformity between the lower and upper succession. The
Caroda Formation of the central Rocky Creek Syncline is
largely devoid of volcanics. A single outcrop only of the
lowermost volcanic horizon in the Caroda Formation of the
Back Creek region, the High Valley andesite tuff (Hocking
1973), has been located and sampled.
The Spion Kop Conglomerate, the lowest unit of the
upper succession, disconformably overlies the Caroda
Formation (Figures 5, 6). The glaciogenic conglomerate 
and diamictite succession of early Namurian age (Opdyke
et al. 2000) have not been sampled in this study for want of
suitable volcanic horizons. The Spion Kop Conglomerate is
overlain in the northern part of the Rocky Creek Syncline
by the Ermelo Pyroclastics with a hornblende K–Ar age of
319 /H110065 Ma and a SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 321.3/H110063.2 Ma
(Figures 5, 6) (Opdyke et al. 2000).
The Clifden Formation of middle to late Namurian age
(Opdyke et al. 2000) overlies the Spion Kop Conglomerate,
or the Ermelo Pyroclastics where present (Figures 5, 6).

### page_7
It is made up of fluvial feldspatholitic sandstone, plant-
bearing siltstone and conglomerate and is characterised 
in the central Rocky Creek Syncline by the Peri Rhyolite,
an ignimbrite with a SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 318.0 /H11006
3.4 Ma (Opdyke et al. 2000). The Peri Rhyolite has been
correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern
Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11).
The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al.
2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006
2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag-
netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified
(Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the
Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’).
This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for
global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that 
the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite,
which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the
Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the
lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse
Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with 
the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow-
ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded
this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver
belonging to the Caroda Formation. Several regionally less
extensive volcanic units occur beneath the Peri Rhyolite in
the Back Creek region near Trevallyn (Figure 4): among
them the Glen Idle Rhyolite (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al.
2000) and an underlying unnamed vitric volcanic horizon.
The Pine Cliffs Road section of the more western Kathrose
Thrust Sheet contains only the upper part of the Clifden
Formation, and the westernmost Darthula Thrust Sheet
contains only its uppermost part (Figure 6).
The Clifden Formation is overlain by the fluvial to 
distinctly glaciogenic Rocky Creek Conglomerate of early
to middle Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6) (Opdyke et al.
2000). The glaciogene rocks are largely restricted to the
upper part of the formation and crop out well along 
the Rocky Creek section within the axial region of the 
central Rocky Creek Syncline. The more prominent 
volcanic horizon is the Plagyan Ignimbrite (Hocking 
1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section has a
well-exposed succession of vitric tuffs and vitric tuffaceous
diamictites in the upper part of the Rocky Creek
Conglomerate. The upper part of the Pine Cliffs Road 
section of the Kathrose Thrust Sheet has been tentatively
correlated (Opdyke et al. 2000) with the lower part of the
Rocky Creek Conglomerate. The westernmost Darthula
Thrust Sheet contains various ignimbrites in the Rocky
Creek Conglomerate, such as the Hazelvale Rhyolite in the
lower part of the formation.
The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark 
Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the
northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the
central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic
horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green
Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000)
near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite
(Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section
is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty 
siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the
Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000).
A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late
Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics
and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek
Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in 
his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous 
volcanics of the Tamworth Belt.
Deformation phases
The New England Orogen has a long history of tectonic
activity . Up to eight tectonic phases have been identified for
the period from Devonian to the Late Cretaceous opening
of the Tasman Sea (Korsch & Harrington 1981; Harrington
& Korsch 1985a; Veevers et al. 1994b; Opdyke et al. 2000). The
Tamworth Belt has been affected strongly by four of the
phases. These may have induced magnetic overprints on
the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir-
ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo-
magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary
and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely
cleaned pseudo-components.
The oldest of these four Carboniferous tectonic phases
relates to development of the erosional disconformity
between the lower and upper succession. Magnetic over-
prints close to the top of the eroded succession may result
from chemical processes during erosion, or may be due 
to fluid-flow that used the erosional disconformity as a 
pathway .
The second tectonic phase had a major effect on the
shape of the New England Orogen. It involved latest
Carboniferous to earliest Permian initiation of the
Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system by extension 
and subsequent formation of the Texas – Coffs Harbour 
and Manning Oroclines. The time of oroclinal deformation
is debated (Aubourg et al. 1994; Klootwijk in press a), with
estimates ranging from latest Carboniferous (Murray et al.
1987), earliest Permian (Fergusson & Leitch 1993), to Late
Permian (Collins 1991). Some agreement is now emerging
for an Early Permian origin as argued by Harrington and
Korsch (1985a; Korsch & Harrington 1987; Harrington 1989;
Lennox & Flood 1997). Fluid movements related to this
major tectonic phase have led to substantial magnetic 
overprinting with a reverse polarity ‘Kiaman’ signature
(Aubourg et al. 1994).
The third phase relates to the Middle Triassic main
phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny , when the Tamworth
Belt overthrusted westward across the Lachlan Orogen
(Korsch et al. 1997). Substantial magnetic overprinting
related to fluid movements can be expected for this phase.
The fourth phase relates to Late Cretaceous initiation
of rifting between Lord Howe Rise and eastern Australia
at ca 95 Ma and opening of the Tasman Sea at ca 84 Ma
(Veevers et al. 1991; Symonds et al. 1996; Müller et al. 2000),
and is probably also related to a thermal event along the
eastern seaboard at ca 105–95 Ma, followed by cooling, uplift
and denudation at ca 95–90 Ma (Schmidt & Embleton 1981;
Moore et al. 1986; O’Sullivan et al. 1999). This opening is
characterised by pervasive magnetic overprinting with
exclusively normal polarity (Cretaceous Normal Polarity
Superchron), widely developed along the eastern seaboard
and also recognised inland, along structural zones in par-
ticular . Its presence is expected in the Tamworth Belt, being
a major zone of prolonged structural weakness.

### page_10
SAMPLING
Sampling strategy
An initial pilot study of the Tamworth Belt succession, on
the Lower Carboniferous volcano-sedimentary succession
of the Upper Rouchel region, demonstrated that ignimbritic
volcanics can retain their primary magnetisation, despite
conditions leading to pervasive overprinting of inter-
calated volcaniclastic rocks. Widespread occurrence of
magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt
1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie &
Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession
and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs
Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well
established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block
concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani-
clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas,
tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon-
iferous succession.
Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian–
Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek
Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three
phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples)
was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic
results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a)
and their implications were discussed in an initial syn-
thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the
Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up 
sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for
comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions
and for fold tests. Sampling was complemented in 1999 with
a small collection (6 sites, 71 samples) to strengthen the
palaeomagnetic record of the Clifden Formation. This 
sampling also addressed the stratigraphic position of the
Boomi Rhyolite – Kooringal Dacite succession, generally
considered part of the Caroda Formation, but interpreted
herein as part of the Clifden Formation.
Samples were collected with a portable drill, an adapted
STIHL auger , using a water jacket for cooling and stainless
steel barrels for reduced magnetic contamination. Standard
drillcores of 2.5 cm diameter and up to 15 cm length were
orientated with an inhouse-developed orientation device
with integrated magnetic and solar compasses and a clino-
meter . Sampling concentrated on stratigraphic sections
through regionally representative structures, to try to avoid
tectonic complications. In general, bedding control for the
volcanic rocks could be determined from intercalated 
volcaniclastic rocks. This was not possible for some sites
of the Ermelo Pyroclastics, but indicative bedding control
was obtained from faint planar indicators in the pyro-
clastics.
Sampled sites
Regional geological detail of the sampled region is shown
in Figure 4, based on Stroud (1990a, b), and site-specific
detail is listed in Table 1. The stratigraphic position of
the sampled sites is indicated in stratigraphic sections
(Figure 6) after J. Roberts (in Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5).
Sampling in the northern Rocky Creek Block concen-
trated on volcanic rocks in the Caroda to Lark Hill
Formations. Prominent volcanic horizons in the Caroda
Formation, that is the Yuendoo Rhyolite and West Lynne
Rhyodacite, were sampled mainly in steeply eastward-
dipping beds on the fault-duplicated western limb of the
Slaughterhouse Syncline (Figure 4) (McKelvey 1968; Yeates
1970; Johnson 1971; Pickett 1994). A single site of the
Yuendoo Rhyolite (site 8) was collected on the eastern limb
of the syncline for a fold test. Several tuffaceous horizons
below the Yuendoo Rhyolite have been sampled on the 
western (2, 3) and eastern (4) limbs of the syncline. In 
general, samples from the West Lynne Rhyodacite showed
weathering effects associated with the Visean–Namurian
hiatus. Site 13, collected on a curved strike ridge, may have
been affected by local rotation along a nearby fault.
Prominent volcanics in the Lark Hill Formation, that is the
Tycannah Rhyodacite and the Tops Ignimbrite, have been
sampled along the gently eastward dipping Tops Road sec-
tion (47–52). Boulders and matrix of a prominent conglom-
erate level (48) have been sampled for a conglomerate test.
Sampling of the Caroda Formation in the central Rocky
Creek Block has been limited to an isolated outcrop of the
High Valley andesite tuff (1) in the Back Creek region
(Hocking 1973) on the western limb of the Rocky Creek
Syncline (Figures 3, 4). In Boomi Creek, directly east of
Trevallyn, a volcanic–volcaniclastic succession has been
sampled (Kooringal Dacite – Boomi Rhyolite: 29–33), which
was mapped as Caroda Formation (Hocking 1973; Stroud
1990a, b; Opdyke et al. 2000). Palaeomagnetic and rock mag-
netic evidence obtained in this study indicates that the 
succession probably belongs to the Clifden Formation
(Figure 6), with the Boomi Rhyolite arguably the equivalent
of the Peri Rhyolite, and with the Boomi Rhyolite –
Kooringal Dacite succession thus constraining the lower
boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Super-
chron.
The Ermelo Pyroclastics (14–21) have been sampled in
several fault-duplicated structures on the eastern limb of
the Rocky Creek Syncline (McKelvey & White 1964; Stroud
1990b). Bedding control was difficult to establish for some
sites (16–18, 20) and had to rely on weakly developed planar
structures.
Sampling of the Clifden Formation, Rocky Creek
Conglomerate and Lark Hill Formation in the Rocky Creek
Syncline has been carried out in well-exposed sections
along Rocky Creek (24, 38–46) and Boomi Creek (25, 28–33,
36, 37), with another section through the Clifden Formation
(22, 23, 27) sampled in a minor creek descending from the
western limb of the Rocky Creek Syncline (Figure 4). A 
further two Rocky Creek Conglomerate sites have been
sampled in the Plagyan Ignimbrite on the southeast flank
of the middle Tertiary Mt Kaputar volcano (34, 35) directly
beneath the Nandewar flows (White 1965).
Sampling of the Kathrose Thrust Sheet has been limi-
ted to five sites. Two Clifden Formation sites (53, 54) have
been sampled along the freshly excavated Pine Cliffs Road
(Figure 4). A further two sites, one along the same road 
section (55) and the other near Llangollan (56), were origin-
ally mapped as Clifden Formation (Hocking 1973; Stroud
1990b), but were identified as Rocky Creek Conglomerate
by J. Roberts (in Opdyke et al. 2000).
Sampling of the Darthula Thrust Sheet (Figure 4) has
been limited to two sections through the Rocky Creek
Conglomerate—a lower section in Boomi Creek directly
west of Trevallyn (57–60) and an upper section near
384 C. T. Klootwijk

### page_11
Darthula (62, 63)—with a further site in the Lark Hill
Formation near Llangollan (64).
MAGNETIC TREATMENT, ANALYSIS AND 
INTERPRETATION METHODS
Sample preparation
All core samples were sandblasted to remove possible mag-
netic contamination from the stainless-steel drill barrels,
and were sliced into standard specimens, 2.54 cm diameter
and 2.2 cm height. Top and bottom of the specimens were
ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities
and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At
least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each
sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen
per sample. Alternating-field (AF) demagnetisation was
carried out on one representative specimen per site and
rock magnetic studies on one other specimen per site.
Palaeomagnetic treatment
One specimen per sample was subjected to progressive 
thermal demagnetisation in 18–36 steps up to peak temper-
atures of 695°C. Thermal demagnetisation was carried 
out in large-volume furnaces (McElhinny et al. 1971) at the
centre of feedback-controlled Rubens–Helmholtz coil 
systems (10 coils), which reduce the ambient magnetic field
to less than 5 nT over the heating–cooling cycle. To 
minimise oxidation, an argon atmosphere was maintained
during the heating cycle (~1 h), but not during forced 
cooling in air (~0.5 h). Depending on initial intensity of
magnetisation and on intensity decrease during demagnet-
isation, remanence measurements were carried out on a 
2-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer (resolution 2 /H1100310
–3
mAm–1), a 3-axis 2G-Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer
(SRM 760R, 10 –2 mAm–1), or a Molspin spinner magneto-
meter (10–1 mAm–1). The access ports of the three magneto-
meters are placed in the centres of 6-coil Helmholtz systems
to reduce systematic pick-up of viscous magnetisation 
during measurement. All magnetometers are connected 
via a LAN to a central database for online data storage 
and retrieval. The system facilitates real-time inspection
of Zijderveld (1967) plots so that informed decisions can 
be made during measurement about continuation of the
demagnetisation treatment. Magnetochemical changes
have been monitored through low-field susceptibility 
measurements with a Digico bulk-susceptibility bridge
after each remanence measurement step. All AF demagne-
tisations were carried out with the automated AF demagne-
tiser attached to the 2G-Enterprises magnetometer in 
27 steps up to 160 mT . All AF demagnetisations above 
25 mT peak value have been subjected to a six-axis cyclic
demagnetisation procedure to counteract possible gyro-
magnetic effects (Giddings et al. 1997). After completion 
of demagnetisation the remanence and susceptibility 
data have been transferred to an ORACLE database on 
the Australian Geological Survey Organisation’s Solaris
SUN Unix system for further processing.
The specimens have been analysed individually for 
linear directions, planar elements and Hoffman–Day
(Hoffman & Day 1978) directions with an interactive 
graphics analysis program, linked to the ORACLE database
and based in part on Kirschvink’s (1980) Principal
Component Analysis method. A three-pass procedure for
directional analysis of multicomponent magnetisations
has been followed. The first two passes have been applied
only for initial interpretation of demagnetisation data for
the pilot specimens of the 1987 collection (approximately
30% of the samples for these 17 sites). The third pass has
been applied to the entire sample collection (64 sites). In 
the first pass, Zijderveld and equal-area plots of demagnet-
isation data for individual pilot specimens have been 
scrutinised with the interactive graphics analysis program
and relevant linear or Hoffman–Day components that
showed a visually acceptable fit to the data have been deter-
mined. This determination has been routinely carried out
in the geographical reference frame. Based on experience,
such a visual analysis of individual specimen results,
although by nature somewhat subjective, is to be preferred
above batch-type analysis of specimens following more
objective, but pre-set and rigid acceptance criteria. In the
second pass, density distributions in geographical and
stratigraphic coordinates of linear and Hoffman–Day direc-
tions determined in the first pass have been scrutinised,
per site or per formation, for concentrations and/or 
distributions that could be interpreted in terms of the
Carboniferous pole path for the Tamworth Belt. In the third
and final pass all specimens, including the pilot specimens
already provisionally interpreted during the first two
passes, have been (re-)analysed following the first pass 
procedure. Site-mean directions have been determined
from linear components and Hoffman–Day components for
a few specimens for which no linear components could be
determined. Finally , pole positions have been determined
for individual sites and for sites grouped per formation or
per stratigraphic interval and have been interpreted in
terms of a meaningful pole path.
Rock magnetic treatment
Various rock magnetic tests have been carried out on 
one representative specimen per site in order to determine
magnetic granulometry and magnetic mineral content.
This involved: (i) the Lowrie–Fuller (Lowrie & Fuller 1971)
test for an indication of domain structure; (ii) the
[(Saturation) isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM)]
acquisition test for magnetic mineral determination;
(iii) the three-axis Lowrie (1990) test for identification 
of magnetically weak minerals in particular; and (iv) 
low-field, low- and high-temperature susceptibility cycling
(Schmidt 1993; Hrouda 1994) for determination of granu-
lometry , identification of magnetic minerals and for an
indication of possible chemical alterations during thermal
cleaning. The first three tests have been carried out on 
the same specimen, which has been cleaned prior to 
each test in the maximum 250 mT field obtainable with 
the automated AF demagnetiser on the 2G-Enterprises
cryogenic magnetometer . The fourth test has been carried
out on hand-crushed powders of one other representative
specimen per site. The Lowrie–Fuller test showed for all
sites, without exception, higher resistance to AF
demagnetisation for weak-field anhysteretic remanent
magnetisation (ARM) than for IRM. This uniformity 
conveys very little, other than adding to doubts about 
Palaeomagnetism of the Rocky Creek Block 385

the applicability of the Lowrie–Fuller test (Dunlop &

IRM ACQUISITION TEST
IRM has been acquired along the z-axis (axial direction) of
the samples. For the 1987 and 1995 collections (Table 1, AI
and CIY/CIB prefixes) IRM has been acquired with a PYE
Scientific Instruments (3/H11032/H11032) electromagnet up to 500 mT and
with the Newport Instruments-E (7 /H11032/H11032) electromagnet up to
2000 mT , 23 steps in total. For the 1999 collection (Table 1,
CIC prefix) IRM has been acquired with the 2G-Enterprises
pulse magnetiser in 24 steps up to 2700 mT . Measurements
have been carried out on a Molspin magnetometer .
LOWRIE TEST
Using the same electromagnets as for IRM acquisition, the
specimens have been magnetised successively along three
orthogonal axes in constant fields of 2000 mT (z-axis),
400 mT (y-axis), and 120 mT (x-axis). The specimens have
then been thermally demagnetised in up to 31 steps up to
685°C in an argon gas environment. Measurements have
been carried out on Molspin and ScT magnetometers.

Magnetic fabric determination
Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility was determined
with the AGICO KLY-3S slow-spinning magnetometer on
magnetically untreated specimens, one per sample and up
to 10 or 12 specimens per site. The KLY-3S operates at 
875 Hz, with a sensitivity of 3 /H1100310
–8 SI for bulk measure-
ments and 2 /H1100310–8 SI for anisotropy measurements. Mean-
tensor coefficients, eigenvalues and error ellipsoids were
determined with AGICO’s ASTA program and also with 
the ANIPO program developed at the Fort Hoofddijk palaeo-
magnetic laboratory , University of Utrecht, the Nether-
lands. Both programs apply Jelinek’s (1978) tensorial
statistics to determine site-mean anisotropy of magnetic
susceptibility (AMS) results, with more flexible data edit-
ing for ANIPO data files (ASCII) versus ASTA ’s (binary).
PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
General component structure
Thermal demagnetisation generally resulted in better
separation of multicomponent magnetisations than AF
demagnetisation. Therefore, thermal demagnetisation was
routinely carried out on at least one specimen per sample.
In general, AF demagnetisation has been limited to one
specimen per site with the results used as a first indication
of the site’s magnetisation content and magnetic behaviour .
All demagnetisations have been carried out as progressive
treatments, allowing full directional analysis of multi-
component magnetisations. An overview of the component
structure follows and representative Zijderveld plots are
presented in Figure 7. Magnetic components are described
in more detail in Appendix 1*.
First-pass inspection of thermal demagnetisation
results indicated the general presence of two thermally 
distinct groups of magnetic components, unblocked at 
low temperatures (LT) and at higher to high temperatures
(HT). Further scrutiny identified a third group of magnetic
components, generally with intermediate unblocking
temperatures (IT) and identified these as overprint mag-
netisations. A few sites showed overprints with high to very
high unblocking temperatures; for convenience these have
been included in the intermediate group.
The LT components are generally removed below 
300°C and below 30 mT . They are nearly exclusively of
normal polarity with in situdirections (mean-site direction:
D = 5.6°, I = –64.5°, n = 54, k = 96.0, /H9251
95 = 2.0°; mean-site pole:
138.3°E, 72.6°S, /H925195 = 2.9°) closer to the present field direction
in the sampled region (D = 11°, I = –60.5°) than to the
expected direction according to the axial geocentric dipole
field model (D = 0°, I = –49°). The HT components are gener-
ally removed between 250° and 680°C and 15–160 mT , and are
predominantly of reverse polarity with downward and
broadly southward directions. Demagnetisation at higher
temperatures (upper magnetite and hematite unblocking
temperature ranges) mainly shows declination rather than
inclination shifts, with appearance of incompletely cleaned

pseudo-components prior to isolation of better cleaned
components at the higher temperature steps. Considerable
effort has been spent in detailing and identifying pseudo-
components and proper components through detailed,
prolonged demagnetisation and statistical analysis. This
demonstrated that the components with the best statistical
parameters (/H9251
95), the preferred primary component repre-
sentatives, were often obtained from the remaining last few
percentages of the magnetic signal (Tables 2, 3). Discon-
tinuation of the demagnetisation procedure at lower
temperatures would have prevented such distinction, risk-
ing determining mean results from less well-cleaned
pseudo-components (Tables 5*, 6*). The third group of IT
components includes various magnetically softer com-
ponents and, for convenience, a magnetically very hard
component. In situ or bedding-corrected directions 
(Table 7*) suggest that these IT components are indicative
of phases of magnetic overprinting of mainly Early
Permian, Permo-Triassic (bedding corrected) and Late
Cretaceous (in situ) age, but also of middle Carboniferous
(bedding corrected), Miocene and Holocene age ( in situ ).
These IT components are generally unblocked between
100°C and 480°C and below 20 mT , with the exception of the
very hard component in the Eulowrie Pyroclastics of the
Lark Hill Formation, which is removed between 570°C and
670°C and between 100 mT and 160 mT .
ROCK MAGNETIC RESULTS
IRM acquisition
The IRM acquisition curves show that the magnetisation
of most of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks is made up
of a magnetite phase, generally saturated in fields of
200–300 mT [e.g. Yuendoo Rhyolite, West Lynne Rhyodacite,
Ermelo Pyroclastics, Glen Idle Rhyolite, Kooringal Dacite,
Plagyan Ignimbrite, Rocky Creek Conglomerate at Rocky
Creek, part of the Eulowrie Pyroclastics, Tycannah
Rhyodacite, part of the Tops Ignimbrite, Pine Cliffs
Rhyolite (Figure 8b), and tuff below the Darthula
Rhyodacite] and sometimes in higher fields [part of the
Yuendoo Rhyolite (Figure 8a)]. A fair number of volcanics,
however , show a distinct high coercivity , hematite or
goethite phase, after saturation of a magnetite phase at
200–400 mT [e.g. the High Valley andesite tuff (Figure 8c),
part of the Yuendoo Rhyolite, Peri Rhyolite, Boomi Rhyolite
(Figure 8d), part of the Eulowrie Pyroclastics, part of the
Tops Ignimbrite, and Darthula Rhyodacite].
Three-axis Lowrie test
A minority of the volcanic rocks shows a distinct goethite
component, obviously weathering related [e.g. West Lynne
Rhyodacite, Ermelo Pyroclastics, Peri Rhyolite (Figure 8f),
Boomi Rhyolite, part of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate and
part of the Tops Ignimbrite]. The volcaniclastic rocks,
being more prone to weathering, show more consistent
presence of a goethite component (e.g. the tuffaceous beds
near the Hazelvale Rhyolite and above the Pound Creek
andesite tuff). Most of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks
show a distinct magnetite unblocking temperature range
[e.g. Yuendoo Rhyolite (Figure 8g), West Lynne Rhyodacite,
Ermelo Pyroclastics, Kooringal Dacite, Peri Rhyolite
(Figure 8f), Boomi Rhyolite, Plagyan Ignimbrite, Rocky
Creek Conglomerate, part of the Eulowrie Pyroclastics,
Tycannah Rhyodacite, Tops Ignimbrite, Pine Cliffs Rhyolite
and most of the volcaniclastic rocks]. A small number of
volcanic rocks show a distinct hematite Curie temperature
up to 675°C [e.g. the High Valley andesite tuff (Figures 8e,
9c), part of the Yuendoo Rhyolite (Figures 8h, 9e), the Pound
Creek andesite tuff, main part of the Eulowrie Pyroclastics,
main part of the Tops Ignimbrite and the Darthula
Rhyodacite], additional to magnetite. The Ermelo Pyro-
clastics and part of the volcaniclastic rocks show distrib-
uted unblocking temperature ranges up to 300°C. None 
of the three-axis Lowrie test results clearly indicate the
presence of maghemite or iron sulfides.
Low-field, low- and high-temperature 
susceptibility cycling
LOW-TEMPERATURE SUSCEPTIBILITY CYCLING
Low-temperature susceptibility cycling shows the typical,
unresolved signature of the multidomain (MD) magnetite
isotropic point at approximately –140°C and the Verwey
Transition at approximately –150°C (Schmidt 1993) in 
various volcanic rocks [some of the Yuendoo Rhyolite 
sites with suspected incomplete separation of an HT com-
ponent and a present field-like component (or an aberrant
HT component direction), West Lynne Rhyodacite, Ermelo
Pyroclastics (Figure 9a), a Peri Rhyolite site, the remagne-
tised Plagyan Ignimbrite sites at Mt Kaputar , the vitric
tuff–diamictite succession of the Rocky Creek Conglomer-
ate (Figure 9b), part of the Eulowrie Pyroclastics of the
Lark Hill Formation, tuffs below and above the Pine 
Cliffs Rhyolite and the tuff directly below the Darthula
Rhyodacite]. However ,the majority of volcanic rocks with
well-defined HT components show no or very limited pres-
ence of MD magnetite (e.g. the High Valley andesite tuff,
most of the Yuendoo Rhyolite, Kooringal Dacite, most of the
Peri Rhyolite, Boomi Rhyolite, the Tycannah Rhyodacite,
the Tops Ignimbrite, the Pine Cliffs Rhyolite and the
Darthula Rhyodacite). The MD magnetite signature shows
up more consistently in the volcaniclastic rocks (e.g. in the
matrix of the conglomerate horizon in the Lark Hill
Formation from the Tops Road section).
There is no clear indication in any of the sites for the
Morin Transition at approximately –20°C, but this may
merely reflect sensitivity limitations of the CS-3 unit in
analysing powders that have not been magnetically concen-
trated. Some of the volcanic rocks show minor , but distinct,
susceptibility peaks between approximately –100°C and
–50°C of unclear origin.

HIGH-TEMPERATURE SUSCEPTIBILITY CYCLING
High-temperature susceptibility cycling shows the pre-
dominant presence of a magnetite component with Curie
temperatures up to 580°C [e.g. for the High Valley andesite
tuff (Figure 9c), the Ermelo Pyroclastics, Kooringal Dacite,
Peri Rhyolite, Plagyan Ignimbrite and vitric tuffs of the
Rocky Creek Conglomerate (Figure 9d)]. This magnetite
component is often accompanied by a hematite component
with Curie temperatures up to 680–705°C (e.g. part of the
Yuendoo Rhyolite, West Lynne Rhyodacite, Eulowrie
Pyroclastics, Tycannah Rhyodacite, Tops Ignimbrite, Pine
Cliffs Rhyolite and Darthula Rhyodacite). The character-
istic changeover (lepidocrocite)–maghemite–magnetite
(Schmidt 1993) is visible in some of the volcanic rocks [e.g.
the Plagyan Ignimbrite (Figure 9f), the tuff below the Glen
Idle Rhyolite and the tuff below the Darthula Rhyodacite].
This is also a common observation in the volcaniclastic
rocks. The volcanic rocks quite commonly show formation
of a substantial magnetite component and less frequently
a possible maghemite component after heating to the 
maximum temperature of ~700°C, indicating ineffective-
ness of the argon environment in preventing magnetic
phase changes.
MAGNETIC FABRIC ANALYSIS
Measurement results
The volcanic rocks show a low anisotropy of magnetic 
susceptibility (AMS). Anisotropy values (P) vary generally
between 1 % and 3% (a normal range for ignimbrites and 
air-fall tuffs: MacDonald & Palmer 1990) and occasionally
up to 5%. The volcaniclastic rocks generally show P values
between 1 % and 4% with the exception of a 9% value 
for the matrix of a conglomerate in the Tops Road section
(Site 58). The volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks show pre-
dominance of oblate over prolate AMS ellipsoid shapes.
Well-defined triaxial ellipsoids are also prominent, but 
various sites do not have a clear magnetic fabric pattern.
The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin-
ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans-
ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from
pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly
Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald &
Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown
that the K
min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents
the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the 
K
max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that
imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic
rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction
with the source expected in the downdip direction of
imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it
can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary
depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation.
The in situ K
max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic
rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north–
south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain
is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of
the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first
glance. However , unfolding of the principal susceptibility
axes according to the attitude of the beds shows that the
magnetic foliation planes (K
max–Kint) essentially agree 
with the palaeohorizontal (Figure 10a) and, importantly ,
shows a substantially improved grouping for the K
min axes
(Figure 10c, d). This strongly indicates that the AMS 
392 C. T. Klootwijk

### page_19
patterns are primary . Formational consistency in K max
directional patterns and variation through the stratigraphy
(Figure 11) supports this. The Caroda and Clifden
Formations show a gross north–south alignment, whereas
the Ermelo Pyroclastics show northwest–southeast align-
ment (Figure 11a). The Rocky Creek Conglomerate, in 
particular , and less so the Lark Hill Formation, in contrast
show variable patterns probably reflecting their higher
energy environment (Figure 11b).
The unfolded magnetic foliation planes of the volcanic
units show an about-even distribution of northern and
southern dips throughout the succession (Figure 10e).
Thus, there is no clear indication from magnetic fabric 
evidence for regionally or temporally persistent imbri-
cation effects, and no definitive conclusion can be drawn
from the AMS results alone on the polarity of transport.
Transport patterns
Regional facies variations, such as thickness of beds,
palaeocurrents and proximal versus distal characteristics,
indicate a western, albeit unidentified, source region for
the volcanic rocks (Leitch 1974; Veevers et al. 1982; McPhie
1987; Roberts & Engel 1987; Scheibner & Basden 1998; Wang
& Roberts 1999). This field evidence makes up for the lack
of AMS control on polarity of transport in the limited 
number of volcanic sites with broadly east–west-aligned
K
max axes, pointing clearly to eastward transport directions.
However ,the Caroda and Clifden Formations show north–
south-trending K max axes patterns for which west-to-
east facies variations are not discriminatory regarding
polarity of transport.
The AMS transport indicators are not conducive to
locating a source region for other than, perhaps, the
Ermelo Pyroclastics. The general north–south trend of
transport directions, in the Caroda and Clifden Formations
in particular , suggests distal rather than proximal source
regions and may reflect the common evolution of transport
directions of further travelled material from following 
dip to become aligned with topographic grain.
Consistency in transport directions per formation
across the three thrust sheets supports the above estab-
lished general agreement in palaeomagnetic directions
between the thrust sheets. Consistent and similar north-
northwest–south-southeast transport directions for the
Peri Rhyolite and Boomi Rhyolite further substantiates

INTERPRETATION
Overprint magnetisations: post-folding
MIDDLE–LATE CENOZOIC OVERPRINTS
A magnetically soft overprint of exclusively normal 
polarity and with in situ directions close to the present 
local field direction is consistently present throughout 
the sites (Figure 12a, b). This component is unblocked 
at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 
30 mT . Its mean direction is indistinguishable from 
a present field component in the southward adjacent
Werrie Block. Both are similar to an overprint observed 
on the south coast of New South Wales and interpreted 
as Early Miocene in age (Nott et al. 1991). This set of over-
prints may be indicative of a regional mid-Tertiary
weathering event, although the overprints’ exclusive 
normal polarity and closeness to the present local field 
direction alternatively may point to a recent viscous 
origin. A few sites also show another , magnetically slightly
harder , component with in situ directions close to the 
present local field (Table 7*; Figure 12c). These are exclu-
sively of normal polarity , with the exception of the
Darthula Rhyodacite (Site 63), which shows a reverse
polarity component in addition to a normal polarity 
component. This slightly harder component is unblocked
between 100°C and 500°C. Some sites (e.g. 45 and 46 of
the Eulowrie Pyroclastics) show inclinations for this
harder component that are steeper than the present local
field direction and closer to the expected direction for the
Late Cretaceous overprint (Figure 12a). Finally , two sites 
on the southeastern flank of Mt Kaputar (34, 35) show 
well-defined IT and HT components with in situ directions
(Figure 12d) comparable to the reverse polarity direction 
of the directly overlying Miocene Nandewar Volcanics
(Wellman et al. 1969).
LATE CRETACEOUS OVERPRINT
The Eulowrie Pyroclastics sites and a few other sites 
(Table 7*) show a characteristic, well-defined, magnetically
very hard, component with in situ directions close to the
expected direction for the Late Cretaceous overprint of
normal polarity (D = 9°, I = –75°), or nudging toward the 
present local field direction (Figure 12e). This component
is generally removed between 580°C and 680°C and obvi-
ously resides in secondary hematite. The Late Cretaceous
overprint is well established in the Australian margin of
the Tasman Sea (Schmidt & Embleton 1981; Klootwijk et al.
in press b), where it is attributed to a thermal event with
subsequent cooling, uplift and erosion prior to initiation
of sea-floor spreading. Fission-track and fluid-inclusion
data indicate acquisition at approximately 95–90 Ma. The
Late Cretaceous normal polarity overprint seems to have
a wider regional presence than originally surmised and has
now been established from fission-track and palaeo-
magnetic studies in more inland regions (Schmidt &
Embleton 1981; O’Sullivan et al. 1999; Klootwijk in press b),
probably induced by fluids propagated along major struc-
tural zones.
Overprint magnetisations: pre-folding
PERMO-TRIASSIC OVERPRINTS
Many of the IT and softer HT components and a minority
of harder HT components, predominantly of reverse 
polarity , show , after correction for bedding, poles in the
southwest Pacific with a wide directional coverage, mainly
to the north, east and south of New Zealand (Table 7*;
Figure 13a). This coverage broadly resembles the outline of
the major Permo-Triassic loop on the Australian cratonic
pole path (Figure 13b) (Klootwijk 1996b). Comparison with
a New England pole path would be preferable for dating of
the components, but this is not available. Post-accretion dis-
placement of the New England Orogen versus the craton,
while unresolved in detail, is not expected to notably affect
such a first-order comparison with the cratonic pole path.
The Australian Permo-Triassic loop is ill defined, and its
extent is probably under defined. The loop’s outline and
extent can be judged from the slightly better defined Indian
pole path, transferred to Australia within Gondwanaland
(Figure 13c) (Klootwijk 1996b). Poles close to the outline of
the Australian–Indian Permo-Triassic loop are likely to
reflect overprinting associated with the Permo-Triassic
Hunter–Bowen Orogeny (Harrington & Korsch 1985b;
Veevers et al. 1994a). Large-scale west-directed thrusting of
the Tamworth Belt across the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney
Basin system occurred during its Middle Triassic main
phase (Korsch et al. 1997), facilitating magnetic over-
printing through fluid movements along developing fault
systems.
EARLY PERMIAN OVERPRINTS
A few components of exclusively reverse polarity , mainly
HT components from silicic diamictites and tuffs in the
Rocky Creek Conglomerate (Table 7*), show very steep
inclinations and poles in general agreement with the Early
Permian segment (Figures 12f, 13b, c) of the Australian pole
path, which is outlined by only a few indicative poles (e.g.
Werrie Volcanics: Schmidt 1988). The main extensional
phase of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system
occurred during the latest Carboniferous and Early
Permian (Tadros 1993; Veevers et al. 1994b; Holcombe et al.
1997), followed shortly by oroclinal deformation of the
southern New England Orogen. The Meandarra Gravity
Ridge (Murray et al. 1989), which can be traced for more
than 1200 km from the southern Sydney Basin through the
Gunnedah Basin (along the western Tamworth Belt) up to
the Taroom Trough of the southern Bowen Basin, was
emplaced during this extensional phase. Fluid movements
associated with this igneous activity may have induced
these sporadic HT overprints. It is unclear what has
localised these overprints in contrast to the widespread
occurrence of Permo-Triassic overprints.
OVERPRINTS VERSUS COMPOSITE COMPONENTS
The Permo-Triassic and Early Permian overprints 
(Table 7*) could be affected by composite unblocking of a

Carboniferous primary magnetisation and a Holocene
overprint, and could thus represent artefacts. The likeli-
hood of this effect has been explored by determining 
angular distances between overprint directions and planes
through bounding component directions. This showed
angular distances of /H113495°( /H113498°, /H1134910°) for 33% (43%, 49%) of

the overprints with IT or soft HT blocking temperature

Conglomerate tests
Component directions of volcanic pebbles and matrix have
been compared for conglomerate sites 48 and 58. Both sites
show distributed HT directions for the volcanic pebbles
[site 48: k = 1.1, /H9251
95 = 141.2°, R = 1.85, n =8 ,R o (8, 99%) = 5.26;
site 58: k = 2.4,/H925195 = 40.5°, R = 6.23, n = 10, Ro (10, 99%) = 5.94]
and far better to well-grouping HT directions for the
matrix, identified as Permo-Triassic overprints (Table 7*).
LT directions close to the present local field are dominant
in the matrix and less so in the volcanic pebbles. The results
demonstrate a positive conglomerate test (site 48: likely
randomness at the 99% confidence level) and capability of
the volcanic pebbles to retain an original magnetisation
under conditions leading to pervasive resetting of the
matrix.
Primary magnetisations
Thermal demagnetisations have been continued routinely
until magnetic intensities reduced below the measurement
limit of the ScT cryogenic magnetometer or , for a few sites,
until development of viscous magnetic phases impeded
remanence measurements. The demagnetisations show
that separation of magnetic components generally contin-
ues until high to very high temperatures with subtle, but
systematic and mainly declinational, changes, and that
detailed analysis is required to distinguish primary com-
ponents from incompletely cleaned pseudo-components.
The Zijderveld plots show the general presence of two 
(P1, P2), occasionally three (P0, P1, P2), HT ‘components’ of
successively harder thermal characteristics (Tables 2, 5*)
that are removed in magnetite and hematite unblocking
temperature ranges between 400°C and 700°C. The magnet-
ically hardest P2 components (Table 2) consistently show a
shift toward more westerly declinations than for the P1
components with little change in inclination (Figure 14a;
Table 3). Mean site results for the P2 components show 
better grouping (Figure 14b; Table 3), improved positive 
fold tests (Table 3) and slightly lower mean inclinations
(Figure 14c; Table 3), compared with the P1 ‘components’
(Tables 5*, 6*). Therefore, the P2 component has been 
taken as the preferred, more precise, representation of
the primary magnetisation, although a minority has 
been interpreted as overprints (Table 7*). The P1 and P0
‘components’ with lower unblocking temperature ranges
have generally been interpreted as incompletely cleaned
pseudo-components (Table 5*) despite their convincingly
positive fold tests (Table 6*), or as overprints (Table 7*).
CARODA FORMATION
High Valley andesite tuff (site 1)
The P2 component is carried by hematite with a blocking
temperature range between 570°C and 680°C. Its pole posi-
tion (a on Figure 15; Table 4) locates close to preliminary
poles for the upper Isismurra Formation of the Rouchel
Block (Klootwijk 1996b figure 12c; 1996a table 1.3). There are
no SHRIMP dates available for the High Valley andesite tuff
nor for the upper Isismurra poles, but this resemblance is
in agreement with available stratigraphic control. The P2
component is interpreted as the primary magnetisation for
the High Valley andesite tuff and, if confirmed, bears 
special importance. It is the oldest pole determined here for

the Rocky Creek Block and is the only result indicating a
northern hemisphere palaeolatitude (6°N). Poles for the P1
and P0 component of the High Valley andesite tuff locate
close to P2 poles for sites of the presumably younger
Yuendoo Rhyolite (Figure 16a–c), but are not interpreted as
related. The P1 pole locates close to P2 poles for sites 7 and
9 of the Yuendoo Rhyolite (Tables 2, 5*; Figure 16a–c), but
their cleaning is thought incomplete (see below). The P1
component is interpreted as a pseudo-component. The 
P0 pole locates close to the main pole for the Yuendoo
Rhyolite, but also near to the Permo-Triassic track (Table 7*;
Figure 13) and is interpreted as a Permo-Triassic overprint.
Yuendoo Rhyolite (sites 5–10)
The P2 components for three sites (5, 6, 8) from both limbs
of the Slaughterhouse Syncline (Figure 4; Table 1) show a
well-defined mean pole position (1 on Figure 15; Table 4)
with a significantly positive fold test at the 99% confidence
level (Table 3) (McFadden 1990), and are taken as the 
primary magnetisation. Sites 7 and 9 with MD magnetite
characteristics, show south pole positions away from 
this main grouping and deflected toward the south pole
(Figure 16c), possibly reflecting incomplete removal of a
reverse Recent (Holocene) field component. The distributed
HT directions of site 10 are probably of lightning origin.
The primary pole (P2) for the Yuendoo Rhyolite is crucial
to definition of the Visean part of the Rocky Creek pole
path and ultimately to interpretation of rotational defor-
mation of the Tamworth Belt. There is good potential to
study additional east-dipping sites, but far less potential for
west-dipping sites with suitable outcrop apparently limited
to the studied site on the eastern limb of the Slaughter-
house Syncline (Figure 4). Primary magnetisations could
not be identified for several tuffaceous horizons below the
Yuendoo Rhyolite (sites 2–4, Table 7*).
West Lynne Rhyodacite (sites 11–13)
Pole positions for these three sites disperse upon bedding
correction and no representative primary magnetisation
direction or pole position could be identified (see 
Appendix 1*).
Ermelo Pyroclastics (sites 14–21)
Two sites only , 14 and less clearly 15 (Table 2), show an inter-
pretable, rather soft, magnetite component of normal
polarity that could be taken as a primary magnetisation 
for reason that its, ill-defined, pole locates close to, and on
the younger side of, the well-defined pole for the Yuendoo
Rhyolite.
CLIFDEN FORMATION AND ROCKY CREEK CONGLOMERATE
Tuff below the Glen Idle Rhyolite (site 22)
Pole positions for the HT components (P0–P2) for this site
fall on a great circle with the pole for the harder (500–580°C)
P2 component close to the well-defined pole position for the
Yuendoo Rhyolite. The IRM acquisition curve indicates the
presence of MD magnetite. In the absence of a fold test it
cannot be established whether this harder P2 component
represents the primary magnetisation or a composite.
Peri Rhyolite (sites 26, 27)/Boomi Rhyolite (site 30) and 
associated tuffs (sites 24, 31–33)
Magnetic component directions, rock-magnetic properties
(IRM acquisition, Lowrie test) and magnetic fabric results
for the Boomi Rhyolite and the Peri Rhyolite are compar-
able, underscoring their lithological similarity . Therefore,
it is suggested, as a proposition testable through SHRIMP
dating, that the Boomi Creek section west of Travellyn was
misidentified as Caroda Formation (Hocking 1973; Stroud
1990b; Opdyke et al. 2000) instead of Clifden Formation, and
that the Boomi Rhyolite is a more proximal equivalent of

### page_26
the Peri Rhyolite. Combination of the well-defined P2
directions for the three sites (26, 27, 30) provides a well-
defined pole (2 on Figure 15, Figure 16d; Table 4) with a posi-
tive fold test (Table 3) interpreted to represent the primary
magnetisation. Inclusion of the less well-defined P2 direc-
tion for a stratigraphically slightly lower tuff (24) does not
improve the pole’s statistics and is not preferred as the
more inclusive representative pole. The mean pole for the
P2 components (480–580°C: Table 4) from three thin tuffa-
ceous horizons (31–33) above the Boomi Rhyolite locates to
the west of the Peri Rhyolite – Boomi Rhyolite pole,
supporting east-to-west younging of the pole path (d on
Figure 15).
Upper Clifden Formation – lower Rocky Creek
Conglomerate (sites 37, 53, 54, 57)
Poles for the P2 components for the four sites locate to the
south-southwest of Australia, with the poorly defined pole
for site 53 located away from the more clustered poles for
the other three sites (3 on Figure 15; Table 2). Notably these
three sites come from three different tectonic units—
Kathrose, Rocky Creek and Darthula Thrust Sheets—and
show a well-defined mean pole (Table 4) with a significantly
(99%) positive fold test (Figure 16e; Table 3).
Rocky Creek Conglomerate (sites 39, 40, 55, 62, 63)
These sites from three different thrust sheets, Rocky Creek
(39,40), Kathrose (55) and Darthula (62,63), show well-
grouped poles with a significantly (95%) positive fold 
test (Figure 16f; Table 3) and a mean pole (4 on Figure 15;
Table 4) to the south of the Great Australian Bight. Good
grouping of poles for sites from the three thrust sheets,
demonstrated by the results for the Rocky Creek
Conglomerate and the upper Clifden Formation – lower
Rocky Creek Conglomerate, indicates absence of signifi-
cant rotational deformation between the thrust sheets.
Lark Hill Formation (sites 41, 44–47, 49, 51, 52)
P2 components for these sites show well-grouped poles
(Table 4) with significantly (99%) positive fold tests 
(Figure 16g, h; Table 3), and an overall mean-site pole to 
the south of the Great Australian Bight (7 on Figure 15;
Table 4), but closer inshore than the pole for the Rocky
Creek Conglomerate. There is, however , a systematic 
difference between poles for the Rocky Creek section and
for the Tops Road with the mean-site pole for the latter 
section closer to the pole for the Rocky Creek Conglomerate
and for the former closer to the Great Australian Bight 
section (Tables 3, 4; 5 and 6 on Figure 15). In the absence of
detailed isotopic or palaeontological dating control it 
is unclear whether these two poles represent different
stratigraphic levels and possibly a pole path trend. The
overall mean-site pole is used in pole path construction.
Polarity
The main objective of this study is to define the 
Carboniferous pole path for the Tamworth Belt.
Magnetostratigraphic constraints on the base of the 
Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron are a fortuitous
by-product. Primary palaeomagnetic results show exclu-

sively reverse polarity (Table 2) with two exceptions: the
Ermelo Pyroclastics, with a tentatively identified normal
polarity (sites 14, 15); and the Kooringal Dacite (29). These
observations agree with the extensive magnetostratigraphic
study of the Rocky Creek and Werrie Block successions 
by Opdyke et al. (2000) (summarised in Figure 5), who 
successfully located the older boundary of the Permo-
Carboniferous Reverse Superchron within the Pinnacles
section of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke 
et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11) to the south of the region studied
here, between the normal polarity Wanganui Andesite
(319.2 /H110062.8 Ma) and the reverse polarity Eastons Arm
Rhyolite (317.8/H110062.8 Ma). There is a qualifier to this location:
a normal polarity ignimbrite apparently overlies the reverse
polarity Wanganui Andesite, but structural complexity
clouds its magnetostratigraphic significance. It could:
(i) represent a normal polarity zone in the basal part of
the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron; (ii) require
redefinition of the base of the Permo-Carboniferous
Reverse Superchron above this ignimbrite; or (iii) represent
a stratigraphic misidentification. Opdyke et al. (2000) cor-
related the Eastons Arm Rhyolite with the Peri Rhyolite
(318.0 /H110063.4 Ma) and evidence is presented here that the 
Peri Rhyolite can be correlated with the Boomi Rhyolite.
The present results contribute to further location of the
Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron base constrain-
ing it between the Ermelo Pyroclastics [normal polarity (N):
321.3 /H110063.2 Ma] and the Peri Rhyolite [reversed polarity (R):
318.0 /H110063.4 Ma], and also between the Kooringal Dacite (N)
and the Boomi Rhyolite (R) in the Boomi Creek section,
which has potential for further refining the location.
DISCUSSION
Comparison with regional palaeomagnetic results
Opdyke et al. (2000) interpreted the directional results of
their extensive, excellently executed, magnetostratigraphic
study on the Carboniferous succession of the Rocky Creek
and Werrie Blocks in terms of pole positions. Two of their
conclusions differ from the interpretations presented here
and warrant commenting. These are: (i) the scatter in 
declinations for Caroda Formation sites of the lower 
succession implies the possibility of modest relative rota-
tions between sites; and (ii) mean directions for formations
of the upper succession–Clifden Formation, Rocky Creek
Conglomerate and Lark Hill Formation of the Rocky Creek
Block and the Currabubula Formation of the Werrie
Block–are remarkably uniform.
The thermal demagnetisation procedures followed by
Opdyke et al. (2000) are more than adequate for magneto-
stratigraphic purposes, although not aimed specifically 
at analysing the hardest few percent of magnetisation.
They identified two magnetisation components: a Recent
Field component ‘ A ’ with low unblocking temperatures, and
a primary component ‘B’. Unblocking temperatures for the
latter commonly range from 400°C to 580°C, but extend
sometimes to above 600°C, with the same directions for
magnetite and hematite contributions. The present results,
in contrast, show subtle, but consistent, differences
between the harder P2 components and the softer P1
pseudo-components, with marked improvement in accu-
racy of mean-site directions (Figure 14b; Table 4), although
not necessarily so for the confidence level of the signifi-
cantly positive fold tests (Tables 3, 6*) for P2 versus P1.
The spread in site-mean directions is considerable for
both Opdyke et al.’s (2000) study and the present study
(Figure 17), with a somewhat wider spread in Opdyke 
et al.’s results. Their study did not specifically address
whether this spread may reflect a directional evolution
through the succession. The positive fold tests (Table 3)
obtained in the present study for individual volcanic 
horizons, stratigraphic sections and formations demon-
strate that the spread reflects an east-to-west younging pole
path structure (Figure 15). This structure is recognisable
also in Opdyke et al.’s (2000 table 3) mean pole positions,
albeit to a lesser extent, and presents a robust alternative
to their view [conclusions (i) and (ii) above] on possible
local rotations expressed in the lower succession and on
directional uniformity through the upper succession.
Pole path
The Carboniferous pole path for the Rocky Creek Block
emerging from this study is very long (Figure 15) and indi-
cates large-scale rotational and latitudinal movements for
the block. The newly defined poles further detail the main
Palaeomagnetism of the Rocky Creek Block 401

jection for (a) P2 components for Rocky Creek Block sites listed
in Table 2 and (b) B-components for Rocky Creek Block sites after

### page_28
features of the preliminary pole path for the Tamworth
Belt, based on pilot results (Klootwijk 1996b figure 13).
However ,the new poles for the upper part of the studied
succession, that is, for the upper Clifden Formation to the
Lark Hill Formation, would require a substantial change
to the shape of the Late Carboniferous westward loop 
on the preliminary pole path, if the pole for the upper
Clifden Formation – lower Rocky Creek Conglomerate (3 on
Figure 15) is indeed taken as primary . This would imply that
the younger limb of the westward loop does not follow a
west-to-east track through the Great Australian Bight, but
would double onto itself at more southern latitudes in
Rocky Creek Conglomerate time (4 on Figure 15) before
moving northward toward the Great Australian Bight in
Lark Hill Formation time (7 on Figure 15). Pole path loops
carry an inherent danger of unrecognised overprints.
The three upper Clifden Formation – lower Rocky Creek
Conglomerate sites (37, 54, 57) are all sampled close to major
fault zones and potential overprinting of pre-folding 
(pre-Middle Triassic) origin, facilitated by fluid flow 
along the fault zones, cannot be ignored. Pending further
definition of Late Carboniferous poles for the correlatable
Currabubula Formation in the southward adjacent Werrie
Block, a primary origin for the upper Clifden Formation –
lower Rocky Creek Conglomerate pole, and with it the 
reality of a Late Carboniferous loop, may be questioned.
Pole positions for the underlying succession, the lower
Clifden Formation and the Caroda Formation, further detail
the Early Carboniferous eastward loop (Figure 15) outlined
on the preliminary pole path (Klootwijk 1996b figure 13).
The Peri Rhyolite and Yuendoo Rhyolite poles (2 and 1 on
Figure 15), in particular , detail the shape of the younger
limb of the eastward loop. The pole position for the High
Valley andesite tuff from the lower part of the Caroda
Formation (a on Figure 15) may provide an important 
backward extension to the pole path for the Rocky Creek
Block. This pole position falls on the older limb of the 
eastward loop and is virtually indistinguishable from pre-
liminary pole positions for the upper part of the Isismurra
Formation of the Rouchel and Gresford Blocks (Klootwijk
1996a; Klootwijk 1996b figure 13). Implications of this 
observation for rotational deformation of the Tamworth
Belt will be explored in another paper .
CONCLUSIONS
Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric 
studies of volcanic and volcaniclastic horizons in the
Carboniferous succession (Caroda Formation – Lark Hill
Formation) of the Rocky Creek Block have shown:
(1) No noticeable rotation between the three major
thrust sheets—the Rocky Creek, Kathrose and Darthula—
of the Rocky Creek Block.
(2) Consistent transport directions in the older succes-
sion, Caroda Formation to Clifden Formation, and more
variable transport patterns in the younger succession,
Rocky Creek Conglomerate and Lark Hill Formation.
(3) Four periods of magnetic overprinting: widespread
overprinting of mid-Tertiary (perhaps Recent viscous)
and Permo-Triassic origin, and more restricted Late
Cretaceous and Early Permian overprinting.
(4) Well-defined primary magnetisation components 
in all studied formations—Caroda Formation, Clifden
Formation, Rocky Creek Conglomerate and Lark Hill
Formation—apart from the Ermelo Pyroclastics. The 
primary components reside in magnetite and/or hematite
carriers.
(5) Subtle, but systematic, directional differences
between softer magnetic components residing mainly in 
the magnetite fraction and harder components residing
mainly in the hematite fraction. The latter , with systemati-
cally smaller /H9251
95 values, have been interpreted as primary
magnetisation components, the former as incompletely
cleaned pseudo-components.
(6) A long Visean to Westphalian, east-to-west young-
ing, pole path trajectory supported by at least four positive
fold tests, three with confidence levels above 95% or 99%.
